findings.title: Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked
findings.body: The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is defined but never called anywhere in the file or by any caller. The corresponding `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) is the one used by `_create_processes` and `_ensure_processes_alive`. Either delete the dead method or wire it up — leaving it in production code is misleading and means future maintainers will assume shard-level restart is supported when it is not.

findings.title: Inconsistent metrics tag key between `wait_produce` and surrounding timers
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` both use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, but the `wait_produce` timer right below uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural). This will create two separate tag dimensions in the metrics backend for the same logical concept, making it impossible to filter or group these timers consistently in dashboards. Use the same key (`shard`) for all three.

findings.title: `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` allows 11 restarts instead of the 10 the name suggests
findings.body: The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS:` and the counter is incremented after the check. So the counter can take the values 0..10 with the check still False, then 11 with the check True. That means the consumer will restart an unhealthy flusher process 11 times before crashing, not 10 as the constant name and original semantics imply. Either rename the constant, change the check to `>=`, or move the increment before the check.

findings.title: `process_restarts` counter never resets, so a long-running consumer is doomed by transient crashes
findings.body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is initialized to 0 in `__init__` and only ever incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive`; it is never reset on successful operation. For a long-lived consumer that is rebalanced occasionally and where the SpanFlusher is reconstructed, this is bounded, but the per-process restart counter is shared across the lifetime of the SpanFlusher object. A single flusher that crashes 11 times over the course of days for transient reasons (deploys, brief OOM kills, broker hiccups) will permanently take down the consumer with no path to recovery short of a full restart. Consider resetting the counter once the process has been healthy for a sustained period.

findings.title: `process_restarts` is incremented before the restart attempt, so failed restarts consume the budget
findings.body: The order in `_ensure_processes_alive` is: check `> MAX`, increment, then `process.kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. If `_create_process_for_shards` raises (e.g., OS resource exhaustion, pickling error), the counter has already been incremented and the next health check will be one step closer to crashing the consumer despite no successful restart ever having occurred. Move the increment to after a successful recreation, or wrap the restart in try/except and only increment on success.

findings.title: Old flusher process is not joined before spawning its replacement
findings.body: `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which spawns a new `SpawnProcess` and stores it in `self.processes[process_index]`. `kill()` only sends SIGKILL; it does not wait for the OS to actually reap the process. Until the old process is reaped it can still be inside its main loop, still flushing segments from Redis and still mutating the shared `process_healthy_since` / `process_backpressure_since` `Value`s. Once the new process is up, both processes will flush the same shards concurrently, producing duplicate Kafka payloads on `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` (idempotency assumptions in downstream consumers are likely broken) and racing on the shared `Value`s. Call `process.join(timeout)` (with a short timeout) before spawning the replacement, or use `process.terminate()` followed by `join()` to give it a chance to exit cleanly first.

findings.title: `max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats 0 as None
findings.body: The `or` falls back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` whenever `max_processes` is falsy. Passing `max_processes=0` (e.g., to explicitly disable the flusher) will instead spin up a process per shard. Use `if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` so that 0 is honored. Additionally, with `num_processes = 0`, the subsequent `for i, shard in enumerate(...): process_index = i % 0` would raise ZeroDivisionError — there is no input validation guarding this.

findings.title: Class docstring says 'one process per shard' but the implementation creates up to `max_processes`
findings.body: The updated docstring states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the constructor takes `max_processes` and defaults it to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. A consumer configured with `--flusher-processes=2` and four shards will create 2 processes, each handling 2 shards. The docstring is therefore misleading; describe the actual semantics (e.g., 'creates up to `max_processes` worker processes, each handling one or more Redis shards').

findings.title: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts setup, not that flushing actually works
findings.body: The new test only verifies that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and that 4 shards are distributed. It does not submit any spans, so it cannot catch regressions where the per-process buffers route reads to the wrong Redis keys, where the multiprocessing Value objects are misbound, where restart logic corrupts `process_to_shards_map`, or where flushes are silently dropped because a process never sees data assigned to its shards. Extend the test to submit spans to at least two different shards and assert they reach the pipe, ideally with assertions that each process only flushed its assigned shards.

findings.title: `time.sleep(0.1)` is silently neutered by the existing `time.sleep` monkeypatch
findings.body: The test sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` near the top, then later adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with a comment saying it gives the flusher 'time to process'. Because `time.sleep` is already monkeypatched, this call is a no-op, so the test is silently relying on the flusher threads happening to run far enough during `step.poll()` to see the drift change. The intent (a real, brief wait) is not what the code does; either remove the misleading `time.sleep` and rely on the existing mock, or restore `time.sleep` around that specific call. The current state will hide real flakiness if the threads ever stop being fast enough.
